I read a long piece on AI automation this week and one idea stuck with me: automate the whole workflow, not the single task.
"Draft an email" is a task. Receiving a lead, checking whether it fits, researching the company, drafting a reply, logging it and scheduling the follow-up is a workflow. That's where the time actually goes.
The author suggests treating an AI agent like a junior colleague: a narrow job description, limited access, a review step, and a record of what it did. Anything involving contracts, payments or hiring stays with a human.
The 30-day plan is simple. Week one, find the repetitive work. Week two, build one small prototype. Week three, test it on real cases. Then decide whether it earned the right to expand.
I'd add one thing: measure outcomes like response time and error rate, not how many things the automation produced.
What's the one weekly bottleneck you would hand off first?

I hope this post is received in the way it’s intended. As advice and encouragement, especially for anyone having a tough time finding work.

With AI, inflation, cutbacks, layoffs, and bias in hiring, there are talented people on here describing hundreds, sometimes thousands, of applications with little or no response.

👎Tailoring every CV.
👎Reaching out directly.
👎Following advice.
👎Trying a different approach.
👎Still getting nowhere.

At what point do you say, “I need to pivot”?

I don’t think there’s a fixed number of weeks or applications. Your finances, responsibilities, and the market you’re targeting all matter.

But you don’t have to wait until you’ve exhausted yourself or your savings to explore a different route.

If several weeks of focused effort aren’t generating conversations, take stock. Speak to people who know your market and will give you an honest view.

Is the issue how you’re presenting your experience? 
The roles you’re targeting? 
Or has demand for that work changed?

Those are different problems, and each needs a different response.

A pivot could mean taking your skills into another industry, considering an adjacent role, widening your search, or doing contract work while you work out the next step.

It doesn’t have to mean starting again.

I think we’re going through a significant shift in how people find work and how businesses bring talent in. That creates uncertainty, but it also opens up possibilities.

AI tools and learning platforms make it easier to learn, test an idea, and build something with a small team or limited capital.  That won’t be the right route for everyone. 

When you need an income, “go and build something” can sound painfully detached from reality.

But if you have some room, start small. Solve a problem you understand. Test whether someone will pay for your help. Give yourself another option alongside the job search.

You don’t need to abandon your experience. You may need to find a different place to apply it.

And needing to change direction isn’t a reflection of your worth. 🙏

A supplier can become very good at doing work that its client is gradually forgetting how to do. That may be acceptable when outsourcing is a deliberate permanent choice. It becomes more troubling when temporary support quietly becomes the operating model.

I ran an embedded talent company before the model became fashionable. We helped clients when building a permanent recruitment team didn’t make sense, but our aim was always to leave them better able to hire without us. External support should build capability as well as provide capacity.

The supplier learns through every cycle while knowledge inside the client can disappear. Mariana Mazzucato describes a similar effect as institutional infantilisation: prolonged outsourcing can leave an organisation progressively less able to operate without external support. The client pays for the learning but may retain very little of it.

An RPO brought in for a hiring surge provides flexible capacity. If it remains embedded for years, recruitment has become an ongoing requirement while the capability remains external. Budget treatment may encourage this: an internal team appears as headcount, while an RPO can sit within procurement spend. Both are operating costs, but the latter can sit outside the headcount budget and be presented as variable capacity.

That flexibility also shifts responsibility for downsizing to the supplier. The client reduces its requirement; the RPO manages the staffing consequences, and its recruiters may bear the insecurity. Where redeployment isn’t possible, costs can extend to households and public support. The client’s savings don’t capture all the consequences of its decision. Who pays belongs alongside what it saves.

Internal leadership changes too. Building capability, developing people and improving decisions can give way to selecting suppliers, monitoring service levels and managing contracts. The leader remains accountable for the outcome while owning progressively less of what is needed to produce it.

This may help explain the insecurity felt by many TA leaders. It isn’t simply the arrival of AI. Volatility encouraged organisations to rent recruitment capacity, making internal teams easier to reduce. As internal knowledge disappeared, dependence on external provision grew and leadership became more precarious. An RPO doesn’t inflict this upon an organisation; it happens when outsourcing is used without a strategy for what should remain inside.

When the supplier leaves, is the organisation better able to perform the work—or merely looking for its next supplier?

This isn't just about cutting costs; it's about highly selective, strategic hiring in a "low-hire, low-fire" market. So, what can candidates do to break through?

Here are 3 actionable tips for candidates in a hiring freeze:

✅ **Shift to Skills-First:** Degrees are less critical. Focus on demonstrating in-demand skills like adaptability, problem-solving, and AI literacy. Companies prioritize quick learners who can add immediate value.

✅ **Target Critical Sectors & Temp-to-Hire:** Essential roles in healthcare, cybersecurity, or renewable energy are often exempt. Consider contract-to-hire roles as a strategic entry point—companies use them to fill needs without permanent headcount impact.

✅ **Be Proactive & Differentiate:** Mass applications won't cut it. Network relentlessly, showcase your work with portfolios, and tailor applications to specific company needs, highlighting how you solve *their* current challenges.

What did my job search actually teach me?

This week, as I prepare for my new role, I’ve been archiving the information, spreadsheets and documents from my job search.

Looking back through everything, there are some pretty startling figures.

📊 3% of rejections received any meaningful feedback.

📊 41% of applications never received any response at all.

📊 71% of direct approaches to companies after seeing roles advertised through LinkedIn never received a reply.

And there was a clear difference between sectors.

Worst responders:
Contract catering companies and their associated recruitment agencies.

Best responders:
Hospitality companies.

The companies where I felt the overall recruitment process was particularly strong were:

Wadworth
Stonegate
The Works
Farmfoods
Co-op

This job search has definitely been more challenging than my last one in 2018.

The obvious difference is AI.

I completely understand the challenges AI creates for recruiters, particularly with the volume of applications it can generate.

But used correctly by candidates, I think it’s a fantastic tool.

I’ve used it to help with:

🔹 Keeping track of applications
🔹 Researching companies and sectors
🔹 Preparing for interviews
🔹 Practising interview questions
🔹 Reviewing and refining CV wording
🔹 Challenging my own thinking

But there’s an important point:

You cannot let AI do all the work for you.

It can’t bring your experiences to life in the way you can. It can’t replace your personality, your knowledge or the understanding you’ve built throughout your career.

There has to be a balance.

The reality is that today’s job market is heavily weighted towards the employer and recruiter.

So if you’re looking for work, you really have to work hard to stand out.

What would I do differently if I found myself job searching in a similar market again?

I’d use exactly the same process and template I’ve developed over the years.

But I would probably start looking much earlier at retraining or developing skills for sectors where there is a genuine shortage of talent.

Most people enter the job market because something has changed.

Their role may no longer be required, their company may be struggling, or the wider market may simply not have enough opportunities.

If you’re prepared to look beyond your existing experience and retrain into an area where demand is strong, you potentially give yourself far more options.

That’s probably one of the biggest lessons I’ll take from the last nine months.

I’m very grateful that the search has now come to an end and I’m looking forward to starting my next chapter.

Hopefully, I won’t be doing this again for a very, very long time.

My next big career event will hopefully be retirement…

And that’s still a long way off! 😂

To everyone still searching: keep going, keep adapting and don’t underestimate the value of investing in yourself.

It’s been a tough paper round 



In 1976 I left London, where I'd been recruiting engineers and inspectors for Iran, and moved to Aberdeen. 

My first lesson in how fast a market can vanish and start somewhere else.

My first Aberdeen client was BP at Sullom Voe. My second was Chevron. We supplied them material controllers.

I recruited through four downturns. 1986. 2008. 2014. 2020. 
Each time I watched good people sit by the phone, then sell up and go.

Uncertainty isn't a political problem. 
It's an apprentice deciding whether to start here. 
A contractor wondering where the next job is coming from. A business owner who can't decide whether to hire, train, or sit tight.

Sitting tight is never free.

I don't do politics. Both sides are usually right about something. But I do believe in jobs.

Today's Press and Journal asks why Scotland's energy strategy is still missing. 

The draft came out in January 2023. Consultation closed that May. Three years and several ministers later, we still don't have it.

The draft proposed a presumption against new oil and gas exploration. Now ministers say they back the North Sea.

Which is it?

I'd rather have a decision I disagree with than no decision at all. 
You can plan around a bad answer. You can't plan around silence.

Look at Norway. Same 78% headline tax rate as us. Reliefs differ, but that's not the point. Companies there know they're wanted, and they know the rules next year will look a lot like the rules this year, which is why they keep investing and keep hiring while we keep consulting.

People can't wait that long. They have mortgages. When the work goes, they go. I've watched it happen four times.

I'm all for new energy. Aberdeen can build it. But a drilling engineer doesn't become a wind tech because someone announces a transition. 
An inspection contractor needs a contract. 
An apprentice needs an employer who'll commit for years.

Same with data centres. AI is about to shake up the jobs market and we're still dithering over projects that create work.

Announcements aren't jobs. Strategies aren't jobs. Consultations definitely aren't jobs.

Yes, Westminster holds licensing and tax. Holyrood can't fix the North Sea on its own. Fine. It can still finish its own strategy.

I don't do recruitment any more. I build software that tries to predict where the next jobs will come from. 
Contract awards, field approvals, shutdown schedules. It's getting rather good at it.

So I asked it when Scotland will publish its energy strategy.

It said: insufficient data.

Three years of consultation, and the machine agrees with the ministers.

Mind the gap.

The companies winning with AI right now aren't the ones buying the most tools. They're the ones who shifted from asking "Can AI do this?" to "Which workflows should AI own, and where do humans stay in charge?"

We're past the chatbot era. The latest shift is agentic AI — systems that don't just answer questions but plan multi-step work, use tools, check their own output, and escalate to a human when the stakes rise. Gartner named multi-agent systems a top strategic trend for 2026. Enterprise AI spending is on track to cross $300B globally, with nearly 40% of work activities becoming automatable.

But here's what most leaders get wrong: they automate tasks when they should be automating workflows. Drafting an email is a task. Receiving a lead, checking fit, researching context, drafting a reply, logging the result, and setting a follow-up — that's a workflow. The value compounds at the workflow level.

The playbook for companies that get it right:
1. Start with strategy, not tools. Map the workflow before you pick the AI.
2. Treat AI agents like junior colleagues with access controls — clear job description, limited permissions, review path, and a record of what they did.
3. Build exception queues. Your agent must know when to stop and ask for help.
4. Keep humans in charge of contracts, payments, hiring, and high-stakes decisions.
5. Measure what matters: completion time, error rate, human edits, and business impact.

The real risk in 2026 isn't that AI replaces your team. It's that your competitors build AI-native workflows faster than you do — and your team is still doing manually what their agents handle before lunch.

The question isn't whether to deploy AI agents. It's whether you're designing the right boundaries around them.

Your recruitment AI can break the rules before it rejects anyone.

Imagine a head of HR at a 2,000-person company who is buying an AI sourcing tool. The demo shows sharper shortlists. Nobody asks where the candidate data came from.

We call this borrowed compliance. When you buy the tool, its data practices become part of your hiring process, yet you never see them. The risk is not only in what the tool decides. It is in how the tool was built and fed.

In November 2024 the UK's ICO published the outcomes of its audits of providers of AI recruitment tools. Its auditors made 296 recommendations and 42 advisory notes. The findings were specific. Some tools let recruiters filter out candidates by protected characteristics. Others inferred gender or ethnicity from a name. The ICO judged those inferences too inaccurate to monitor bias, and found they were often processed without a lawful basis or the candidate's knowledge. Some tools also collected far more personal information than they needed.

The EU treats the same use case with more weight. AI used for recruitment and selection is listed as high-risk under the AI Act, and the high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Employers using such a system are deployers, and deployers carry their own duties, including human oversight by people with real authority. The UK and the EU differ in law. They agree on the question: can you explain how this tool treats a candidate?

Before signing, ask three questions, and write the answers into the contract. Where did the candidate data come from, and on what lawful basis? What does the tool infer about candidates, and can that be switched off? Who can overrule a ranking, and is the override recorded?

If you cannot get answers to those three questions before you sign, that is where we start.

The boardroom always gets weird when smart people start debating whether a machine has a soul.
By then the invoice is already due, the policy is already written, and somebody's job just got routed through a server rack with better branding than judgment.

People love the magic trick. They want to argue about "consciousness" because it sounds profound and keeps them safely away from accountability. Cute. The real issue is behavior. What the system is allowed to decide, who signed off on it, and which ordinary man gets buried under the paperwork when it goes sideways.

A company does not get a pass because the spreadsheet was automated. A lender does not get moral amnesty because the denial came from code. A leadership team still owns the decision, even if they dressed it up in sleek language and parked it inside a deck with twelve colors and no courage.

Picture a founder who hires a polished executive to run operations. The executive smiles, misses payroll, mangles contracts, and blames the software. Every man in the room knows the truth. Bad outcomes with a polished explanation still wreck lives.

I say that as a guy who enjoys efficiency a little too much. If a dashboard can clear my calendar and tighten a forecast, my inner operator starts grinning like a fool. Then I remember that convenience is a petty little idol when it starts replacing judgment, responsibility, and plain old backbone.

The coming fight over AI has very little to do with philosophy and everything to do with stewardship. Men should care because behavior shapes paychecks, truth, hiring, lending, security, and the kind of world we hand the next man coming up behind us. A tool with no character in the hands of people with no limits becomes a quiet tyrant.

Ask one hard question every time AI shows up in the room. Who answers when this thing harms someone?

Because somewhere a man is staring at a bank statement, a contract, or a rejection notice, and he deserves a human name on the decision.

Headline: A 200 OK response doesn't always mean your API is working correctly. 🛑

We've all been there. The endpoint returns a 200, but the data is wrong, the system is slow, or a downstream service is broken.

As this great infographic by ByteByteGo shows, true API reliability goes far beyond a basic ping. Here are the 9 essential types of API testing every developer and QA engineer should know:

1️⃣ Smoke Testing: The basic health check. Does it return a 200 OK? (Basic availability).
2️⃣ Functional Testing: Does the output match the requirements? Validating behavior against expected results.
3️⃣ Contract Testing: Do the Consumer and Provider agree on the data format? Ensures requests/responses match the schema.
4️⃣ Integration Testing: Does the API play nicely with others? Validating workflows across dependent services (e.g., Order ➡️ Inventory ➡️ Payment).
5️⃣ Regression Testing: Did your new code break old features? Comparing v1 to v2.
6️⃣ Load Testing: Can it handle the expected traffic? Measuring latency under a steady-state load.
7️⃣ Stress Testing: Where is the breaking point? Ramping up traffic until throttling or 5xx errors occur.
8️⃣ Security Testing: Is it locked down? Verifying auth, access control, and data protection.
9️⃣ Fuzzing Testing: How does it handle garbage? Probing malformed inputs and edge cases to uncover hidden bugs.

Building a resilient system means layering these tests. You wouldn't ship a car without testing the brakes, the engine, AND the crash safety.

Is AI really killing IT contracting? 

The numbers tell a more complicated story. 

Here are four common myths: 

1️⃣ "Nobody's hiring contractors any more." 

The RECs index for IT contractor demand hit 52.7 in August 2026 (anything above 50 means growth). That's its highest reading since April 2023. 

2️⃣ "AI is just a buzzword in job adverts." 

According to IT Jobs Watch, 5,341 UK contract jobs cited AI in the six months to 2 October 2026, up from 1,606 a year earlier. That's 9.73% of all UK contract jobs, up from 4.85%. 

3️⃣ "Put AI on your CV and your day rate will soar." 

The median quoted rate for contract jobs citing AI was £560 a day. But adding "ChatGPT" to your skills list wont get you there. 

4️⃣ "AI is the only skill that matters now." 

Recruiters are still reporting shortages of contractors in cybersecurity, cloud computing, software engineering and security-cleared IT. 

AI isn't replacing good contractors. But contractors who couple real domain expertise with practical, provable AI delivery are leading the charge. 

Are you seeing more AI in your contract briefs, or is it mostly buzzwords?
